answer: I read garnet's current default calibration (set f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade) and looked at every connected 3-qubit chain. The best chain is QB11-QB12-QB7, with QB12 in the middle. The two CZ fidelities are 0.998693 (QB12-QB11) and 0.998016 (QB12-QB7). Their product is about 0.996712. The two best pairs on the chip happen to share QB12, which is why they form the winning chain. I then built a GHZ circuit on exactly those physical qubits (QB11, QB12, QB7). It uses one Hadamard-style rotation on QB11, then a CNOT built from a CZ plus rotations on pair QB12-QB11, then the same on pair QB12-QB7. It measures all three qubits. I ran it on garnet:mock with 200 shots as job 01a1603e-fc29-75ee-8b50-1c80dd9467de. The counts were 000: 46, 011: 54, 100: 54, 111: 46. This is not a GHZ result. A GHZ state should give only 000 and 111, and the mock does not simulate the circuit. It returns placeholder counts, so these numbers say nothing about the circuit or the chain. To see real GHZ behavior you would run on the real garnet, where noise would add some 001, 010 and similar outcomes. The principle is that entanglement is built from two-qubit gates, so picking the qubits with the best two-qubit gate fidelity gives the cleanest state. The chain's gate fidelity product is a rough estimate of how much of the ideal state survives, before readout and single-qubit errors.
